# About this tutorial

ScreenR was written for shRNA screens, but CRISPR-Cas9 knockout screens
produce the same kind of data: a table of read counts, one row for each guide
RNA (sgRNA) and one column for each sample. In ScreenR an sgRNA is simply a
"barcode", and everything in the other tutorials applies. This tutorial goes
through a CRISPR dropout screen step by step and shows what is specific to
CRISPR:

1. installing ScreenR and, optionally, CRISPRcleanR;
2. describing a time-course dropout screen (T0 and later time points);
3. choosing the thresholds on the number of sgRNAs per gene;
4. checking the quality of the screen with essential and non-essential
   reference genes;
5. correcting the copy-number bias of CRISPR-Cas9 with CRISPRcleanR;
6. finding the hits, using the non-essential genes as reference;
7. positive-selection screens.

| | shRNA screen | CRISPR-Cas9 knockout screen |
|---|---|---|
| Reagent (a "barcode" in ScreenR) | shRNA | sgRNA |
| Reagents per gene | often 5 to 25 | usually 3 to 6 (4 in TKOv3 and Brunello) |
| Typical design | treated vs control at each time point | late time point vs T0 or plasmid |
| Gene-independent effects | seed (off-target) effects | DNA cutting: copy-number and proximity bias |
| Good null reference | non-essential genes | non-essential genes (non-targeting sgRNAs do not cut, so they are not a good null) |

# Installation

ScreenR is on Bioconductor:

```{r install-screenr, eval = FALSE}
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages("BiocManager")
}
BiocManager::install("ScreenR")
```

The copy-number correction uses the
[CRISPRcleanR](https://github.com/francescojm/CRISPRcleanR) package (Iorio et
al. 2018). It is optional: everything else in this tutorial works without it.
CRISPRcleanR is not on CRAN or Bioconductor, so it is installed from GitHub;
`BiocManager::install()` also installs its Bioconductor dependencies:

```{r install-crisprcleanr, eval = FALSE}
BiocManager::install("francescojm/CRISPRcleanR")
```

`crisprcleanr_available()` tells whether it is installed:

```{r packages, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(ScreenR)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

```{r available}
crisprcleanr_available()
```

The plots of ScreenR have no theme of their own; one is chosen for the whole
tutorial with `theme_set()`:

```{r theme}
theme_set(theme_light(base_size = 12))
```

```{r no-crisprcleanr, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
if (!crisprcleanr) {
    cat("*CRISPRcleanR is not installed where this tutorial was built: the",
        "code of the copy-number correction is shown but not run, and its",
        "results are read from a precomputed table.*\n")
}
```

# The data

`hap1_count_table` comes from a genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 knockout screen of
HAP1 cells with the TKOv3 library (Hart et al. 2017): the T0 sample and three
replicates after 3 and 18 days of growth. Cells that lose a gene needed for
growth (an essential gene) are lost over time, so the sgRNAs of essential
genes are depleted at day 18. To keep the package small the dataset is a
subset of the 70,877 sgRNAs of the library (see `?hap1_count_table`).

```{r data}
data(hap1_count_table)
data(hap1_annotation_table)
head(hap1_count_table)
head(hap1_annotation_table)
```

The annotation has the gene of each sgRNA and its position in the genome
(used by CRISPRcleanR), and a Class column that tells the core essential and
non-essential reference genes, the controls and the other genes.

# Creating the ScreenR object

The sample names (`T0`, `T3_A`, ...) do not follow the
`Day_Treatment_Replicate` convention of ScreenR, so the samples are described
with a `sample_table`. In a dropout screen the comparison is between time
points, so all the samples belong to the same experiment (`Day = "Screen"`)
and the time point is used as the `Treatment`; the `groups` (used by the
statistical models) are the time points too. The `palettes` give each time
point (and each sample) the same color in every plot.

```{r object, message = FALSE}
samples <- data.frame(
    Sample = colnames(hap1_count_table)[-1],
    Day = "Screen",
    Treatment = c("T0", "T3", "T3", "T3", "T18", "T18", "T18")
)
samples
time_colors <- c(T0 = "#999999", T3 = "#7570B3", T18 = "#D95F02")
object <- create_screenr_object(
    table = hap1_count_table,
    annotation = hap1_annotation_table,
    groups = factor(samples$Treatment, levels = c("T0", "T3", "T18")),
    sample_table = samples,
    palettes = list(
        Treatment = time_colors, Group = time_colors,
        Sample = c(T0 = "#999999", T3_A = "#9E9AC8", T3_B = "#7570B3",
            T3_C = "#54278F", T18_A = "#FDAE6B", T18_B = "#D95F02",
            T18_C = "#A63603")
    )
)
object <- remove_all_zero_row(object)
object
```

# How many sgRNAs per gene?

Several functions test a gene only if it has enough barcodes:
`number_barcode` in `find_camera_hit()`, `find_roast_hit()`,
`find_time_hit()` and `plot_barcode_hit()` (genes need *more than*
`number_barcode` barcodes, default 3) and `min_barcodes` in
`find_gene_zscore_hit()` (genes need *at least* `min_barcodes`, default 3).
These defaults were chosen for shRNA libraries. `barcodes_per_gene()` shows
what the library has:

```{r per-gene}
per_gene <- barcodes_per_gene(object)
table(per_gene$NBarcodes)
```

Most genes have 4 sgRNAs. With `number_barcode = 3`, genes that lost one
sgRNA (and genes designed with 3) are not tested; when this excludes many
genes the functions give a warning that suggests a better value, so it is
safe to start from the defaults. Here `number_barcode = 2` (at least 3
sgRNAs) keeps almost every gene.

# Quality control

The general quality control of [Tutorial 2](Tutorial_2_Quality_control.html)
applies to CRISPR screens, with any sample names and time points.

## Sequencing depth

`plot_mapped_reads()` shows the number of reads of each sample. Samples with
far fewer reads than the others are less reliable:

```{r mapped-reads, fig.height = 3.5}
plot_mapped_reads(object)
```

The T0 sample was sequenced about twice as deeply as the others, which is
common: it is the reference of every comparison. Every sample has at least
1.6 million reads, more than 100 for each sgRNA of this subset.

`plot_mapped_reads_distribution()` shows the distribution of the reads of the
sgRNAs in each sample:

```{r mapped-reads-distribution, fig.height = 3.5}
plot_mapped_reads_distribution(object)
plot_mapped_reads_distribution(object, type = "density", alpha = 0.3)
```

The counts are raw, so the T0 sample, sequenced more deeply, is shifted to
the right. At day 18 the distribution is wider than at day 3, with more
sgRNAs close to 0: the sgRNAs of the essential genes are dropping out.

## Library representation and replicates

The library should be evenly represented at T0 (low Gini index) and the
replicates should agree:

```{r gini, fig.height = 3.5}
plot_gini(object)
```

The plots so far use the raw counts. The correlation between replicates and
the sample plots below compare normalized counts, so the counts are
normalized first (counts per million; the choice of the normalization is
discussed below):

```{r normalize}
object <- normalize_data(object)
```

```{r replicates, fig.height = 5, fig.width = 6}
plot_replicate_correlation(object)
```

## Clustering of the samples

`plot_mds()` and `plot_pca()` place the samples so that similar samples are
close, and `plot_explained_variance()` shows how much of the differences
between the samples each principal component explains. Both the MDS and the
PCA use the log2 normalized counts, with the normalization chosen in
`normalize_data()` (here counts per million), so that the sequencing depth
of the samples does not drive the result:

```{r mds, fig.height = 3.5}
plot_mds(object)
plot_pca(object)
```

```{r explained-variance, fig.height = 3.5}
plot_explained_variance(object)
plot_explained_variance(object, cumulative = TRUE)
```

The first dimension of both plots orders the samples by time point (T0,
then day 3, then day 18): the main difference between the samples is the
growth of the cells, as expected in a dropout screen. The day 3 replicates
are very close; the day 18 replicates differ more, because the depletion has
had more time to diverge. The first principal component explains
`r round(100 * compute_explained_variance(object)[2, "PC1"])`% of the
variability.

## Quality with reference genes

The most informative check of a dropout screen uses genes whose behaviour is
known: the core essential genes should be depleted, the non-essential genes
should not. `hart_reference_genes` has the lists of Hart et al. for human
cells. `compute_screen_quality()` measures how well the two groups are
separated (NNMD and Cohen's d: more negative is better; ROC AUC: 0.5 is no
separation, 1 is perfect) and `plot_reference_separation()` shows it.

```{r reference-genes}
data(hart_reference_genes)
essential <- hart_reference_genes$Gene[
    hart_reference_genes$Class == "core essential"]
nonessential <- hart_reference_genes$Gene[
    hart_reference_genes$Class == "non-essential"]
```

`compute_metrics()` computes the log2 fold change of each sgRNA between two
groups of samples (`control` and `treatment` are values of the Treatment
column):

```{r quality, message = FALSE}
day3 <- compute_metrics(object,
    control = "T0", treatment = "T3", day = "Screen"
)
day18 <- compute_metrics(object,
    control = "T0", treatment = "T18", day = "Screen"
)
quality <- bind_rows(
    `Day 3` = compute_screen_quality(day3, essential, nonessential),
    `Day 18` = compute_screen_quality(day18, essential, nonessential),
    .id = "Time point"
)
knitr::kable(quality, digits = 3)
```

After 3 days the essential genes are only starting to drop out; after 18
days the separation is almost perfect.

```{r separation, fig.height = 3.5}
plot_reference_separation(day18, essential, nonessential) +
    ggtitle("Day 18 vs T0")
```

`plot_boxplot()` shows the normalized counts of the sgRNAs of single genes in
each sample, for example two core essential genes and the EGFP control
(sgRNAs that target a gene not present in the cells):

```{r boxplot, fig.height = 3.5}
plot_boxplot(object,
    genes = c("POLR2L", "RPL14", "EGFP"),
    group_var = c("T0", "T3", "T18"), fill_var = "Treatment", ncol = 3
) +
    scale_x_discrete(guide = guide_axis(angle = 45))
```

The sgRNAs of the essential genes are depleted at day 3 and almost gone at
day 18; those of EGFP are stable (slightly higher, because of the CPM
normalization described below).

`plot_trend()` follows the same genes over time. The time points are in the
Treatment column (`time_column`), and `time` places them at their real days,
so that day 3 is close to T0 and far from day 18:

```{r trend, fig.height = 3.5}
plot_trend(object,
    genes = c("POLR2L", "RPL14", "EGFP"), group_var = c("T0", "T3", "T18"),
    time_column = "Treatment", time = c(T0 = 0, T3 = 3, T18 = 18),
    trend = "mean", ncol = 3, scales = "free_y"
) +
    labs(x = "Days", y = "Mean normalized counts per sgRNA")
```

`plot_barcode_heatmap()` shows each sgRNA in each sample (log2 normalized
counts minus the mean of the sgRNA): every sgRNA of the two essential genes
drops out, which is what a good knockout looks like. A gene supported by a
single sgRNA would show one blue row among white ones.

```{r heatmap, fig.height = 4}
plot_barcode_heatmap(object, genes = c("POLR2L", "RPL14"),
    column_group = "Treatment") +
    scale_x_discrete(guide = guide_axis(angle = 45))
```

The non-essential genes have a positive mean log2 fold change
(`r round(quality$MeanNonessential[2], 2)` at day 18) although they have no
effect. This is a side effect of the CPM normalization: when many sgRNAs drop
out, the reads of the sample go to the others, which look enriched. The
ranking of the genes does not change, but the baseline is not 0. Normalizing
to the sgRNAs of the non-essential genes (`method = "control"`) puts it back
at 0:

```{r quality-control-normalization, message = FALSE}
nonessential_sgrnas <- intersect(rownames(object),
    hap1_annotation_table$Barcode[hap1_annotation_table$Gene %in% nonessential])
day18_control <- normalize_data(object,
    method = "control", control_barcodes = nonessential_sgrnas
) %>%
    compute_metrics(control = "T0", treatment = "T18", day = "Screen")
knitr::kable(compute_screen_quality(day18_control, essential, nonessential),
    digits = 3)
```

The rest of the tutorial uses the CPM normalization. The baseline matters for
the self-contained tests such as FRY, which ask whether a gene changes at all:
with the non-essential sgRNAs at 0, the small real effects of many genes
become significant. In this dataset, normalizing to half of the non-essential
genes made FRY call about 6% of the other half at 5% FDR, against almost none
with CPM. The tests that compare each gene with the others (CAMERA and the
Z-score tests) depend much less on the baseline.

# Copy-number bias and CRISPRcleanR

Cas9 cuts the DNA, and cells with many cuts grow less. sgRNAs that target
amplified regions of the genome therefore deplete the cells whatever the gene
they target, and the genes there look essential. CRISPRcleanR (Iorio et al.
2018) finds the regions where many neighbouring sgRNAs that target different
genes are depleted together and corrects their fold changes, without needing
copy-number data. `correct_crispr_bias()` runs CRISPRcleanR on a ScreenR
object and returns a new ScreenR object with the corrected counts. ScreenR
does not reimplement the method: it only calls CRISPRcleanR.

The correction needs

* the **complete genome-wide library**: CRISPRcleanR assumes that most of the
  genes in a region have no effect. On a subset of genes enriched in hits it
  removes real signal, so it must not be used on `hap1_count_table`;
* a **library annotation** with the position of each sgRNA, in the format of
  CRISPRcleanR (row names: the sgRNA identifiers; columns GENES, CHRM,
  STARTpos and ENDpos). CRISPRcleanR includes the annotation of several
  libraries (`KY_Library_v1.0`, `Brunello_Library`, `AVANA_Library`,
  `GeCKO_Library_v2`, ...); for another library, build the data frame from
  its annotation file.

This example uses the complete HT-29 screen distributed with CRISPRcleanR
(KY library, about 90,000 sgRNAs; HT-29 cells carry an amplification of the
MYC region on chromosome 8q24). It takes about a minute.

```{r crisprcleanr, eval = crisprcleanr, message = FALSE}
ccr <- "CRISPRcleanR"
# Library annotation and counts distributed with CRISPRcleanR
library_annotation <- get(utils::data("KY_Library_v1.0", package = ccr))
counts <- read.delim(system.file("extdata", "HT-29_counts.tsv",
    package = ccr
))
colnames(counts) <- c("Barcode", "Gene", "Plasmid", "HT29_R1", "HT29_R2",
    "HT29_R3")
ht29 <- create_screenr_object(
    table = counts[, -2], annotation = counts[, c("Barcode", "Gene")],
    groups = factor(c("Plasmid", "Late", "Late", "Late")),
    sample_table = data.frame(
        Sample = c("Plasmid", "HT29_R1", "HT29_R2", "HT29_R3"),
        Day = "Screen", Treatment = c("Plasmid", "Late", "Late", "Late")
    )
)
ht29_corrected <- correct_crispr_bias(ht29,
    library_annotation = library_annotation,
    control = "Plasmid", treatment = c("HT29_R1", "HT29_R2", "HT29_R3")
)
ht29_corrected
```

The corrected object is analysed like any other: normalize it, compute the
data table and find the hits. CRISPRcleanR's own results (the corrected
sgRNA fold changes and the segments of the genome) are in
`S4Vectors::metadata(ht29_corrected)$crisprcleanr`.

The effect of the correction on this screen (computed with the code above;
the script is in the `benchmark/crispr` folder of the GitHub repository):

```{r crisprcleanr-results}
correction <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "crisprcleanr_ht29.csv",
    package = "ScreenR"
))
knitr::kable(correction, digits = 3,
    col.names = c("Counts", "NNMD", "Cohen's d", "ROC AUC",
        "Mean log2FC in 8q24 (genes not known to be essential)")
)
```

Before the correction, the genes in the amplified 8q24 region that are not
known to be essential are depleted (mean log2 fold change about -0.26); after
the correction they are not (about 0). The separation of the reference genes
is similar, with a slightly lower ROC AUC: the correction removes a
gene-independent bias, it does not make the screen stronger.

# Finding the hits

The hit-finding functions are used as in
[Tutorial 3](Tutorial_3_Finding_hits.html). The comparison is day 18 against
T0:

```{r design}
design <- create_design_matrix(object)
contrast <- create_contrast(design, treatment = "T18", control = "T0")
```

## Gene-level Z-score test with the non-essential genes as reference

`find_gene_zscore_hit()` compares the mean score of the sgRNAs of each gene
with the scores of random sets of sgRNAs. By default the random sgRNAs come
from all the genes, which include the hits, so the test is conservative when
many genes have an effect, as in proliferation screens. When genes known to
have no effect are available, they are a better reference (`control_genes`).
For CRISPR screens the non-essential genes are the natural choice: their
sgRNAs cut the DNA like any other, while non-targeting sgRNAs do not.

To be able to check the result, here half of the non-essential genes are used
as reference and the other half is kept to count the false calls; in a real
analysis use all of them.

```{r zscore-reference}
set.seed(2017)
reference <- sample(nonessential, length(nonessential) %/% 2)
held_out <- setdiff(nonessential, reference)
statistics <- compute_barcode_statistics(object, design, contrast)
zscore <- find_gene_zscore_hit(statistics,
    control_genes = reference, fdr = 1, seed = 1
)
head(zscore)
```

```{r zscore-evaluation}
called <- zscore$Gene[zscore$FDR <= 0.05]
data.frame(
    `Genes called` = length(called),
    `Core essential` = sum(called %in% essential),
    `Held-out non-essential` = sum(called %in% held_out),
    `Other genes` = sum(!called %in% c(essential, nonessential)),
    check.names = FALSE
)
```

Almost all the `r length(essential[essential %in% hap1_annotation_table$Gene])`
core essential genes of the dataset are found at 5% FDR, with very few of the
held-out non-essential genes. The other genes called are not in the reference
lists: HAP1 cells need many more genes than the core essential set, which
contains only the genes essential in almost every cell line.

## Without reference genes: the empirical null

When no reference genes are available, `reference = "empirical"` estimates
the scores of the genes without effect from the data. Most genes have no
effect, so the centre of the distribution of the gene statistics is the null;
a normal distribution is fitted there and gives the p-values. The hits, in
the tail, do not widen it. `empirical_fit = "one-sided"` estimates the spread
from the side without hits only (above the centre for depleted genes), which
gives more power when the hits are well separated, as in CRISPR screens; the
default, `"central"`, is the safer choice (see `?find_gene_zscore_hit`).

```{r zscore-empirical}
zscore_empirical <- find_gene_zscore_hit(statistics,
    reference = "empirical", fdr = 1
)
zscore_one_sided <- find_gene_zscore_hit(statistics,
    reference = "empirical", empirical_fit = "one-sided", fdr = 1
)
attr(zscore_one_sided, "null")
```

`plot_empirical_null()` shows the gene statistics and the fitted null, which
should follow the centre of the distribution; the depleted genes are in the
tail on the left:

```{r empirical-null-plot, fig.height = 3.5}
plot_empirical_null(statistics, empirical_fit = "one-sided")
```

## Other methods and their consensus

The other methods need no reference genes either: the default reference of
the Z-score test (random sets of sgRNAs of all the genes), CAMERA and FRY.
`number_barcode = 2` keeps the genes with 3 or 4 sgRNAs.

```{r other-methods}
zscore_default <- find_gene_zscore_hit(statistics, fdr = 1, seed = 1)
camera <- find_camera_hit(object, design, contrast,
    number_barcode = 2, fdr = 1
)
fry <- find_roast_hit(object, design, contrast,
    method = "fry", number_barcode = 2, fdr = 1
)
hit_list <- list(zscore_reference = zscore,
    zscore_empirical = zscore_empirical,
    zscore_one_sided = zscore_one_sided, zscore = zscore_default,
    camera = camera, fry = fry)
hits <- summarise_hits(hit_list, fdr = 0.05)
head(hits)
table(hits$NMethods)
```

`plot_common_hit()` shows how the hits of the methods overlap (an UpSet
plot, since there are more than three methods; each column counts the genes
found by exactly the combination of methods marked below it):

```{r upset, fig.height = 5, fig.width = 9}
plot_common_hit(hit_list, fdr = 0.05,
    title = "Depleted genes at day 18 (5% FDR)")
```

How many of the hits are core essential, and how many are held-out
non-essential genes (false calls):

```{r other-methods-evaluation}
evaluate_hits <- function(result) {
    called <- result$Gene[result$FDR <= 0.05]
    data.frame(
        `Genes called` = length(called),
        `Core essential` = sum(called %in% essential),
        `Held-out non-essential` = sum(called %in% held_out),
        check.names = FALSE
    )
}
knitr::kable(bind_rows(lapply(hit_list, evaluate_hits), .id = "Method"))
```

The empirical null finds almost as many core essential genes as the
non-essential reference, without reference genes and with very few held-out
non-essential genes. The two tests that compare each gene with all the others
(the default Z-score test and CAMERA) are much more conservative: they find
less than half of the core essential genes, and the default Z-score test does
not give a p-value below 0.05 to any of the held-out non-essential genes.
Their reference is all the genes of the library, and here it is full of hits:
the subset keeps all the reference genes, so
`r round(100 * mean(per_gene$Gene %in% essential))`% of its genes are core
essential, against about 4% in the complete TKOv3 library. They remain
conservative on the complete library: there the default Z-score test found
58% of the core essential genes at 5% FDR, the empirical null 90%
(`"central"`) and 94% (`"one-sided"`), and the non-essential reference 96%.
The default Z-score test and CAMERA rank the genes almost in the same way
(Spearman correlation of the p-values above 0.99).

FRY (`find_roast_hit()`) tests each gene on its own sgRNAs. It estimates the
variability from the replicates of the model, so a single T0 sample is
enough when the other time points have replicates, as here. It finds more
essential genes than the tests without reference, with very few held-out
non-essential genes.

## Comparable fold changes

`scale_by_reference()` scales the fold changes so that the non-essential
genes are at 0 and the essential genes at -1. Scaled values can be compared
between screens of different strength, for example between cell lines or time
points:

```{r scale}
scaled <- scale_by_reference(day18, essential, nonessential)
scaled %>%
    group_by(Gene) %>%
    summarise(ScaledLog2FC = mean(ScaledLog2FC)) %>%
    arrange(ScaledLog2FC) %>%
    head()
```

# Positive-selection screens

In a drug-resistance or positive-selection screen the interesting genes are
**enriched**: their knockout makes the cells survive. Every hit-finding
function takes `direction = "Up"`:

```{r up, eval = FALSE}
find_gene_zscore_hit(statistics, direction = "Up")
find_camera_hit(object, design, contrast, direction = "Up")
```

The reference genes are not useful there (they describe fitness, not
resistance); use the default reference of `find_gene_zscore_hit()` or control
genes known to have no effect on the selection.

# Summary

| Step | CRISPR-specific advice | Functions |
|---|---|---|
| Create the object | describe time points with a `sample_table` | `create_screenr_object()` |
| sgRNAs per gene | lower `number_barcode` / `min_barcodes` for 3-6 sgRNAs per gene | `barcodes_per_gene()` |
| Quality control | check the separation of essential and non-essential genes | `compute_screen_quality()`, `plot_reference_separation()`, `plot_trend()`, `plot_barcode_heatmap()` |
| Copy-number bias | correct with CRISPRcleanR on the complete library | `correct_crispr_bias()` |
| Hits | use the non-essential genes as reference when available, otherwise the empirical null | `find_gene_zscore_hit(control_genes = )`, `find_gene_zscore_hit(reference = "empirical")`, `plot_empirical_null()`, `find_camera_hit()`, `find_roast_hit()`, `summarise_hits()`, `plot_common_hit()` |
| Compare screens | scale to the reference genes | `scale_by_reference()` |
| Positive selection | look for enriched genes | `direction = "Up"` |

# Literature

* Hart T, Brown KR, Sircoulomb F, Rottapel R, Moffat J (2014). Measuring
  error rates in genomic perturbation screens: gold standards for human
  functional genomics. Mol Syst Biol 10:733.
* Iorio F, Behan FM, Goncalves E et al. (2018). Unsupervised correction of
  gene-independent cell responses to CRISPR-Cas9 targeting. BMC Genomics
  19:604.

# Session info

```{r session-info}
sessionInfo()
```
